cards.q: What replaces coding puzzles in the internal A3 assessment?
cards.a: A committee defense of your real project work, scored against the competency matrix.

cards.q: Name the 5-part structure for presenting your project.
cards.a: Problem, constraints, 2–3 design options with tradeoffs, chosen design rationale, measured outcome.

cards.q: Who gates the assessment attempt?
cards.a: Your manager (sponsorship) plus a readiness review.

cards.q: What is the single biggest defense mistake?
cards.a: Describing team achievements with "we" and never owning a decision with "I".

cards.q: What do window functions do that GROUP BY cannot?
cards.a: Keep every row while computing a value over a related frame — no collapse.

cards.q: Name the canonical dedup pattern for latest record per key.
cards.a: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY ts DESC, id DESC)`, keep rn=1.

cards.q: RANK vs DENSE_RANK on scores 100, 100, 90?
cards.a: RANK: 1,1,3 with gaps; DENSE_RANK: 1,1,2 without.

cards.q: Why are aggregates illegal in WHERE?
cards.a: WHERE filters rows before grouping; group-level filters belong in HAVING.

cards.q: What silently turns a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN?
cards.a: A WHERE predicate on the right table's column — move it into ON.

cards.q: What does a 1.1x duplicate join key do to a revenue SUM?
cards.a: Fans out rows and silently doubles the total.

cards.q: How do you stop CTE recomputation?
cards.a: Snowflake: `WITH t AS MATERIALIZED`; Spark: `CACHE TABLE` to pin intermediates.

cards.q: File won't fit in memory — expected plain-Python answer?
cards.a: Stream it with a generator: yield, don't return.

cards.q: When do you choose PySpark over pandas?
cards.a: Over ~10 GB, multi-file/Parquet input, cross-dataset joins, or explicit distribution requirements.

cards.q: Name two causes of driver OOM.
cards.a: `collect()` and `toPandas()` pulling full results into driver RAM (also oversized `take()`).

cards.q: Name three causes of executor OOM.
cards.a: One giant partition (skew), `repartition(1)` before a heavy stage, cache without MEMORY_AND_DISK.

cards.q: Relative cost of native vs pandas vs Python UDFs?
cards.a: Native 1×; pandas UDFs ~2–5× via Arrow batches; Python UDFs ~10×+.

cards.q: How do you fix a skewed groupBy?
cards.a: Salt the hot key into N buckets and aggregate in two stages; or let AQE split skewed partitions.

cards.q: When is cache() justified?
cards.a: Only when a DataFrame is reused ≥2× — persist MEMORY_AND_DISK, then unpersist.

cards.q: When does CAP actually force a choice?
cards.a: Only during a network partition — before that you get both consistency and availability.

cards.q: State the quorum rule and what it guarantees.
cards.a: R + W > N forces read/write overlap so reads see the newest write; W > N/2 prevents split-brain.

cards.q: Availability of W=3/R=3 vs W=1/R=5 on N=5?
cards.a: 99.1% on both paths vs ~99.999% writes and 59.0% reads.

cards.q: Why are duplicate deliveries guaranteed?
cards.a: Retries are mandatory, so delivery is at-least-once — duplicates are normal, not exceptional.

cards.q: What does "exactly-once" actually mean?
cards.a: Effectively-once end-to-end: idempotent producer, transactional offsets, and a sink participating in commit.

cards.q: Why do windows close on event time + watermarks?
cards.a: Wall clocks lie across machines; event time plus watermarks make closes deterministic despite disorder.

cards.q: Why is 2PC a poor fit across services?
cards.a: It blocks — a crashed coordinator leaves locks held; use sagas with compensating transactions.

cards.q: What does the ingestion layer do?
cards.a: Only transport — no business logic; the choices are pull vs push and full vs incremental.

cards.q: Why is log-based CDC the OLTP default?
cards.a: Captures hard deletes at minimal source overhead with seconds latency; polling misses deletes, triggers slow every write.

cards.q: What belongs in bronze?
cards.a: An immutable, append-only raw copy plus ingest metadata — replay insurance, never edited downstream.

cards.q: What happens to rows failing the silver quality gate?
cards.a: Quarantined with reason and lineage — gold stays clean; fix upstream and replay.

cards.q: Name the #1 data-modeling question.
cards.a: Declare the grain — e.g. "one row per order line."

cards.q: Why does SCD2 preserve as-of analytics?
cards.a: The fact's surrogate FK pins it to the dimension version true at event time — expire + insert in one transaction.

cards.q: Name the data-observability pillars.
cards.a: Freshness, volume, schema, distribution, lineage.

cards.q: What is the real batch-vs-streaming tradeoff?
cards.a: Latency vs reprocessing/state cost — never throughput.

cards.q: Latency floors of micro-batch vs true streaming?
cards.a: Spark Structured Streaming ~500 ms; Flink/Kafka Streams 10–100 ms.

cards.q: Define the watermark.
cards.a: W = maxObservedEventTime − allowedLateness — a monotonic promise; the window emits when W passes its end.

cards.q: Why can one idle partition freeze all windows?
cards.a: W is the min across partitions, so a stalled source stalls watermark progress everywhere.

cards.q: What happens to an event later than allowed lateness?
cards.a: Side output or dead-letter queue; within lateness, re-accumulate and re-fire as a retraction.

cards.q: Fraud SLA under 5 s — batch or streaming?
cards.a: True streaming; an hourly dashboard gets cheap batch, in between micro-batch.

cards.q: Name the three layers that must align for exactly-once.
cards.a: Replayable source, exactly-once checkpointed state, transactional or idempotent sink.

cards.q: Why did data lakes fail?
cards.a: Structurally — no atomic commits, schema enforcement, compaction, or governance; the swamp, not bad engineers.

cards.q: Name the layers that compose a lakehouse.
cards.a: Open Parquet files + transactional table format + object storage + catalog — any engine on top.

cards.q: How does Snowflake prune without user partition keys?
cards.a: ~16 MB micro-partitions carry automatic min/max metadata for pruning.

cards.q: What did cloud DWs trade away?
cards.a: Openness — proprietary formats, and lake + warehouse means two copies of data plus lock-in.

cards.q: When does ETL still beat ELT?
cards.a: At trust boundaries: PII masking before load and cross-region compliance.

cards.q: Auto-suspend or always-on — the utilization rule?
cards.a: Under 30% → per-second auto-suspend; over 60% sustained → always-on or reserved.

cards.q: What is data mesh, honestly?
cards.a: An org model for ownership — centralize the substrate, decentralize product ownership.

cards.q: Deepest architectural difference between the platforms?
cards.a: Storage ownership: Snowflake bundles it; Databricks keeps your lake as source of truth in your bucket.

cards.q: Why did Databricks SQL become competitive?
cards.a: Photon — C++ vectorized execution over Delta.

cards.q: How do the billing models differ?
cards.a: Credits bundle IaaS with 60 s minimum; DBUs stack on top of the underlying VM bill.

cards.q: Cost of all-purpose vs jobs DBU misclassification?
cards.a: About 3× — $0.55 vs $0.15 per DBU.

cards.q: Contrast the lock-in shapes.
cards.a: Snowflake locks data gravity; Databricks locks workflows — the data stays in your bucket.

cards.q: How should you treat vendor benchmarks?
cards.a: They contradict by workload shape — run a 2-week PoC on your schemas and query mix.

cards.q: Neutral layer for sharing data between both engines?
cards.a: Iceberg tables plus one REST catalog — Open Catalog/Polaris or Unity.

cards.q: What does a table format add over bare Parquet?
cards.a: Atomic commits, updates/deletes, schema/partition evolution, and pruning metadata over immutable files.

cards.q: Describe Delta's metadata structure.
cards.a: One `_delta_log` of JSON commits with a Parquet checkpoint every 10th commit.

cards.q: Walk the Iceberg metadata tree.
cards.a: Catalog CAS pointer → metadata.json → manifest list → manifests → data files, pruned at each level.

cards.q: What is Iceberg hidden partitioning?
cards.a: Transforms like `days(ts)` live in the spec — engines never hand-write partition filters; evolution is metadata-only.

cards.q: Name the four delete strategies by cost ladder.
cards.a: CoW rewrites, position deletes, deletion-vector bitmaps, MoR log records — write cost falls, read cost rises.

cards.q: When is data actually deleted?
cards.a: Only by VACUUM/expire_snapshots/clean — time travel is replay, not deletion.

cards.q: Commit size of one 400-row UPDATE across formats?
cards.a: Delta/Iceberg ~KBs via DVs; Hudi CoW ~100 MB rewritten; Hudi MoR ~50 KB log append.

cards.q: Fundamental model difference between Spark and Flink?
cards.a: Spark runs incremental micro-batches; Flink processes record-at-a-time, with batch as a bounded stream.

cards.q: Latency floor of each engine?
cards.a: Spark ~the batch interval (0.5–10 s); Flink ~10 ms.

cards.q: What is a Flink checkpoint?
cards.a: An asynchronous Chandy–Lamport barrier snapshot — barriers ride the data, processing never pauses.

cards.q: When do you enable unaligned checkpoints?
cards.a: Under backpressure — barriers overtake in-flight buffers and snapshot them too; bigger but steady duration.

cards.q: Name Flink's exactly-once assembly.
cards.a: Rewindable source + barrier-aligned snapshot + TwoPhaseCommittingSink committing on notifyCheckpointComplete.

cards.q: When does AQE split a skewed partition?
cards.a: Above 256 MB and 5× the median — into ~64 MB subtasks, no code needed.

cards.q: Why TTL on every keyed Flink operator?
cards.a: Unbounded keyed state is the #1 production killer.

cards.q: What does AQE re-plan with, and since which release?
cards.a: Actual shuffle stats at each Exchange boundary — default since Spark 3.2.

cards.q: State both AQE skew-join split triggers.
cards.a: Partition above 5× the median AND above 256 MB — split toward ~64 MB subtasks.

cards.q: Why doesn't AQE fix skewed groupBy?
cards.a: Skew split covers joins only (SMJ/SHJ) — aggregate skew needs salting.

cards.q: Broadcast join condition and its failure mode?
cards.a: One side ≤ 10 MB per honest stats; stale/underestimated stats make the driver OOM collecting it.

cards.q: How do you size shuffle partitions?
cards.a: ≈ shuffle bytes ÷ 128–256 MB — over-provision, AQE coalesces; the 200 default is wrong both ways.

cards.q: Storage vs execution memory under pressure?
cards.a: Storage evicts blocks; execution never evicts — it spills to disk.

cards.q: What does max task time ≫ p50 in the UI mean?
cards.a: Skew; uniformly slow tasks point to sizing, spill, or GC instead.

cards.q: What third model does Kafka add beyond queue and pub/sub?
cards.a: A partitioned, replayable append-only log with consumer-owned offsets.

cards.q: What ordering does Kafka guarantee?
cards.a: Strict order only within a partition — key hashing fixes per-entity order.

cards.q: State the canonical Kafka durability recipe.
cards.a: acks=all + RF=3 + min.insync.replicas=2 + unclean.leader.election disabled.

cards.q: Define the high watermark.
cards.a: The highest offset replicated to all ISR — consumers read only up to it.

cards.q: Why is dual-writing DB + Kafka wrong?
cards.a: A crash in between loses the event with no record — use the outbox pattern with CDC.

cards.q: Where is exactly-once real in Kafka?
cards.a: Inside Kafka — idempotent producer + transactions + read_committed; across boundaries, at-least-once + idempotent sinks.

cards.q: Name two rebalance-storm fixes.
cards.a: Cooperative-sticky assignor and static membership (group.instance.id).

cards.q: Name the six data-quality dimensions.
cards.a: Accuracy, completeness, freshness, validity, uniqueness, consistency.

cards.q: What runs at each data-test-pyramid layer?
cards.a: Unit tests every PR, data tests every run, reconciliation daily, production monitoring continuous.

cards.q: What happens when a quality gate fails?
cards.a: Circuit breaker — publish to staging, promote atomically so consumers keep last-known-good.

cards.q: When should quarantine alerts fire?
cards.a: When the quarantine rate exceeds ~1% — never drop records silently.

cards.q: Error budget for 99% freshness over 30 daily runs?
cards.a: 0.3 runs — so page on the very first miss.

cards.q: What makes a backfill idempotent?
cards.a: DELETE + INSERT per partition or MERGE — same input, same output, never blind append.

cards.q: Name the incident loop stages.
cards.a: Alert, classify, contain, fix, backfill, verify, blameless postmortem — each incident adds a check.

cards.q: What job does each of the five sources do?
cards.a: Wiki explains, handbook curates, SDE builds, DET community, DEC practitioner benchmarks.

cards.q: How big is the canonical reading list?
cards.a: Four books plus two papers, each tied to a course section — not the 25-book firehose.

cards.q: Required read-to-build ratio, and the failure it prevents?
cards.a: 1:2 — prevents tutorial hell, where the 40th Spark video compounds to zero.

cards.q: What is the build spine?
cards.a: API → ingest → lake → transform+DQ → serve → ops — one repo, layers added weekly.

cards.q: How many portfolio projects should you finish?
cards.a: One archetype — a small finished repo with a README of tradeoffs.

cards.q: What is drill 15 and why does it matter?
cards.a: A 5-minute walkthrough of your design doc — it IS the A3 architecture screen.

cards.q: What does the internal design round probe?
cards.a: Your own project (Scenario 0) plus hypothetical extensions — scored on narrative + evidence.

cards.q: Name the six answer-framework steps.
cards.a: Clarify, estimate, high-level design, tradeoffs, ops and failure, evolution.

cards.q: Why state the freshness SLA first?
cards.a: It decides the architecture — sub-second means Kafka+Flink; sub-minute allows a committing lakehouse sink.

cards.q: What replaces STAR in defense prep?
cards.a: The evidence ledger: claim → story → artifact → metric → matrix line — 4–5 stories, 90 seconds each.

cards.q: Storage math for 100k ev/s at 500 B with RF=3?
cards.a: 4.32 TB/day raw → ~13 TB replicated → 6 brokers × 4 TB, 48 partitions at ~1 MB/s.

cards.q: Why is exactly-once not correctness?
cards.a: Checkpoints/2PC are processing semantics only — dedup windows and reconciliation handle late, wrong, or fraudulent data.

cards.q: Golden invariant of a warehouse-to-lakehouse migration?
cards.a: No consumer ever sees wrong data — waves ordered by consumer, gated on 7 days under 0.01% delta.

cards.q: What is the repeating framework across all 11 GenAI design chapters?
cards.a: Clarify requirements → frame as ML task → data preparation → model development → evaluation → overall system design, with deployment + monitoring on top.

cards.q: How do you pick the generative model family?
cards.a: Requirements arithmetic: one-pass latency → GAN/VAE, ceiling quality → diffusion, resolution at scale → autoregressive tokens, video economics → latent diffusion.

cards.q: Why retrieval (RAG) before finetuning for knowledge injection?
cards.a: Finetuning can't cite sources and needs constant retraining; RAG balances cost, scalability, freshness — RAFT finetuning only after retrieval is fixed.

cards.q: What must accompany offline metrics in a GenAI evaluation answer?
cards.a: Online business metrics — CTR, adoption, cost per user per month — because users re-roll failed generations and burn GPU money; name both unprompted.

cards.q: Name the 7-step ML design framework.
cards.a: Clarify, frame as ML task, data prep, model development, evaluation, deployment/serving, monitoring.

cards.q: Why not optimize raw clicks?
cards.a: Clicks reward clickbait and completions bias short videos — name failure modes, choose relevance-aware objectives.

cards.q: Why reject GBDT in continual-learning systems?
cards.a: It cannot be fine-tuned — every refresh means retraining from scratch.

cards.q: Walk the ranking-metric elimination chain.
cards.a: MRR ignores post-first hits, recall@k drowns in millions, precision@k is rank-blind — use nDCG or mAP.

cards.q: Where do business rules belong in serving?
cards.a: In re-ranking — never baked into the model.

cards.q: Why weight unobserved pairs in matrix factorization?
cards.a: Observed-only loss reaches zero with degenerate all-ones embeddings — WALS forces real separation.

cards.q: What does NCE below 1 indicate?
cards.a: The model's cross-entropy beats the background-CTR baseline — calibration before serving to auctions.

cards.q: Why encoder-decoder for translation?
cards.a: Bidirectional source understanding, natural variable-length I/O, cross-attention into encoder output.

cards.q: Why masked LM, not next-token, in pretraining?
cards.a: Full-sentence input with next-token prediction lets the encoder leak the answer.

cards.q: How does BPE handle unseen words?
cards.a: Rare words decompose into known subword pieces; `</w>` marks word boundaries.

cards.q: How are named entities handled?
cards.a: Replaced with ENTITY_1-style placeholders before training, restored after decoding.

cards.q: Why beam search over top-k/top-p?
cards.a: Deterministic same-input-same-output and higher accuracy — diversity is a defect in translation.

cards.q: Which metric matches synonyms via WordNet?
cards.a: METEOR — harmonic mean of precision and recall, best human-judgment correlation.

cards.q: What routes input when language is unknown?
cards.a: An encoder-only language-detection classifier routes to the per-pair model.

cards.q: Name the three training stages.
cards.a: Pretraining, supervised finetuning, RLHF — knowledge, response behavior, human alignment respectively.

cards.q: Why rank instead of score responses?
cards.a: Absolute numeric scores drift between annotators; rankings become (prompt, winning, losing) preference pairs.

cards.q: Why RoPE over absolute positional encoding?
cards.a: Absolute encodings trained at 512 break at 4096; RoPE captures relative position geometrically.

cards.q: Default decoding for open-ended chat?
cards.a: Top-p (nucleus) sampling with tuned temperature — deterministic search loops in dialogue.

cards.q: Why does top-k fail?
cards.a: Fixed k misfits the distribution — sharp loses the obvious token, flat caps diversity.

cards.q: Name the evaluation layers.
cards.a: Perplexity, task benchmarks, safety benchmarks, human plus online signals (LMSYS Arena).

cards.q: How do follow-ups work?
cards.a: Session management feeds chat history into the prompt enhancer's context.

cards.q: Frame image captioning as an ML task.
cards.a: Translation with pixels as the source language — image encoder, decoder-only Transformer emits the caption.

cards.q: Per-patch tokens or one global vector?
cards.a: Per-patch sequence — attention needs sequences and a global vector discards local detail.

cards.q: Name three cleaning steps for the 400M pairs.
cards.a: Dedup via perceptual hash/CLIP, CLIP relevance filter below ~0.25, LLM summarization of long captions.

cards.q: Why summarize long captions before training?
cards.a: The model imitates caption length — long training captions produce long, unusable suggestions.

cards.q: Why beam search over sampling?
cards.a: Higher quality, deterministic same-image-same-caption, coherent — diversity is unwanted.

cards.q: How are ambiguous images handled?
cards.a: Beam-search cumulative probability below a confidence threshold disables the suggestion.

cards.q: What is CIDEr and its blind spots?
cards.a: TF-IDF vectors, cosine similarity vs references, averaged; blind to novel phrasing and word-order semantics.

cards.q: Why RAG over finetuning for document QA?
cards.a: Knowledge changes often and citations are required — finetuning can't stay current or provide references.

cards.q: Why AI-based over rule-based parsing?
cards.a: Varied single/double-column layouts break fixed templates — layout detection plus OCR reads boxes in order.

cards.q: Compute chunks for 5M pages.
cards.a: 1,500-char pages, 500-char chunks with 200 overlap → 5 text + 3 image chunks/page ≈ 40M chunks.

cards.q: What is the shared embedding space contract?
cards.a: The same encoder embeds chunks and queries; CLIP or captioning aligns images.

cards.q: Why is exact nearest-neighbor search infeasible?
cards.a: O(N×D) — 40M comparisons per query; ANN is ~O(log N×D).

cards.q: Name the RAG triad.
cards.a: Context relevance, faithfulness, answer relevance.

cards.q: When do you RAFT-finetune?
cards.a: Only after retrieval is fixed — golden plus distractor docs teach the LLM to ignore noise.

cards.q: Why GAN over diffusion here?
cards.a: One forward pass meets the <1s SLA, and the structured latent space enables facial attribute manipulation.

cards.q: Why normalize pixels to −1..1?
cards.a: It matches the generator's final Tanh activation — a ReLU output would mismatch the range.

cards.q: Name the three GAN training failures.
cards.a: Vanishing gradients, mode collapse, failure to converge.

cards.q: Fix for mode collapse?
cards.a: Wasserstein loss or an unrolled GAN.

cards.q: When does GAN training stop?
cards.a: When discriminator accuracy nears 50% — past it, feedback becomes coin flips and quality degrades.

cards.q: Why random over truncated latent sampling?
cards.a: Diversity matters for faces; truncation buys realism at diversity's cost.

cards.q: Which metric is lower-is-better?
cards.a: FID — Fréchet distance between real and generated feature distributions.

cards.q: Why autoregressive over diffusion here?
cards.a: Chunked AR is 256 token steps (seconds); diffusion is O(T·N²) with more steps at high res — minutes.

cards.q: What is posterior collapse and the fix?
cards.a: A powerful decoder ignores its latents at high res; discrete codebook tokens force it to use them.

cards.q: Name the four Stage I tokenizer losses.
cards.a: Reconstruction, quantization, perceptual, adversarial — pixel fidelity, codebook commitment, features, realism.

cards.q: How do gradients flow through the quantizer?
cards.a: Straight-through — nearest-neighbor has no gradient, so decoder gradients copy to the encoder.

cards.q: Token math for 1024×1024?
cards.a: 64×64 px per token → 256 sequential generation steps.

cards.q: Why split generation and decoding services?
cards.a: Distinct computational profiles and latencies — each scales independently.

cards.q: How is 2048² served?
cards.a: Generate at 1024², then a pretrained 2× super-resolution upscaler (RCAN/ESRGAN).

cards.q: Why diffusion over autoregressive for text-to-image?
cards.a: Superior fine detail plus a tunable sampling-steps dial — complexity traded for quality.

cards.q: What does the model predict during training?
cards.a: The noise ε, not the clean image x₀ — predicting x₀ underperforms.

cards.q: How does the prompt steer denoising?
cards.a: Cross-attention — queries from image features, keys/values from text-encoder embeddings.

cards.q: Name the two sampling fixes.
cards.a: Classifier-free guidance for prompt adherence; DDIM cuts steps from 1,000 to ~20.

cards.q: Why cascade super-resolution?
cards.a: Diffusion can't generate high resolution directly — train low, upscale 64→256→1024.

cards.q: Why two safety gates?
cards.a: Prompt filtering before compute misses model-generated harm — output harm detection catches it after generation.

cards.q: Which online metric reveals hidden dissatisfaction?
cards.a: Average cost per user per month — unhappy users re-roll seeds, compounding compute spend.

cards.q: Why tuning-based over tuning-free?
cards.a: Identity preservation is the product — 10–20 images give richer identity than one reference image.

cards.q: Rank the three methods by identity fidelity.
cards.a: DreamBooth (full finetune) > LoRA (low-rank delta) > textual inversion (one token embedding).

cards.q: Why DreamBooth despite GB-per-subject storage?
cards.a: 15-min finetune fits the <1h async SLA and models are discarded after the 50 headshots.

cards.q: Why a rare token instead of a common word?
cards.a: Common words carry meanings the model must overwrite; rare tokens are distinct yet tokenizer-cohesive.

cards.q: Name the two DreamBooth losses.
cards.a: Reconstruction on "[V] person" plus class-specific prior preservation on "a person".

cards.q: Why add generic face images to training?
cards.a: Prevents overfitting to one identity and forgetting the generic face class.

cards.q: Why isn't CLIP enough for identity?
cards.a: CLIP/DINO score semantics and detail, not identity — a face recognition model closes the gap.

cards.q: Why latent diffusion for video?
cards.a: VAE compresses 8× spatial and 8× temporal — 512× smaller, making training and inference affordable.

cards.q: Pixel-space cost of a 5s 720p video?
cards.a: ~7 minutes per video on an H100 — 120 frames at 3.6× image pixels.

cards.q: Why precompute and cache latents?
cards.a: Per-step VAE encoding stalls training — ~200 TB cache for 100M videos buys it back.

cards.q: Why DiT over U-Net for video?
cards.a: 3D patchify with Transformer scaling and modality flexibility — Sora and Movie Gen chose it.

cards.q: How do you handle scarce video–text pairs?
cards.a: Fold images in as single-frame videos — one joint training stage.

cards.q: Which metric catches flicker?
cards.a: FVD — Fréchet distance over I3D features; FID/IS score frames and miss motion.

cards.q: Name the two super-resolution stages.
cards.a: Spatial SR restores 720p; temporal SR interpolates 12 FPS to 24 FPS.

terms.def: Event-time progress marker; windows close and late data is judged against it.
An operation safe to retry — same input, same final state, no duplicate effects.
Effect semantics built from at-least-once delivery + idempotent writes or transactional commits.
Bronze (raw) → silver (validated) → gold (business-ready) layering of lakehouse data.
Retrieval-augmented generation — ground an LLM answer in retrieved documents.
Dense vector representation of text/image such that semantic similarity ≈ vector distance.
Adaptive Query Execution — Spark re-plans joins/partitions at shuffle boundaries using runtime stats.
In-sync replicas — Kafka followers caught up enough to acknowledge writes.
Columnar file format with per-column encoding and nested-type support.
Change data capture — stream of row-level changes from an OLTP log.
Slowly changing dimension keeping history as new versioned rows.
Reprocessing historical data with new logic into the same destination.
Batch + speed layers serving merged views; Kappa collapses both onto one stream.
Redistributing data across partitions between stages; the dominant Spark cost.
Uneven key distribution making one partition dominate stage time.
Durable snapshot of Flink state enabling exactly-once recovery.
Merging small files into fewer large ones to restore read performance.
Multi-column clustering of lakehouse files to prune scans on any column.
Broadcast vs sort-merge vs shuffle-hash — picked by size + skew stats.
Versioned repository of point-in-time-correct features for training and serving.
Distributed log-based messaging system; topics are split into ordered, replicated partitions.
Distributed compute engine executing a DAG of stages and tasks across executor JVMs.
Streaming-first engine with event-time windows, keyed state, and checkpointed exactly-once pipelines.
Fully managed cloud warehouse separating storage, virtual warehouses, and cloud services.
Lakehouse platform built on Spark with Delta Lake, collaborative notebooks, and managed ML tooling.
Open table format adding ACID transactions and a transaction log on top of Parquet.
Open table format with hidden partitioning, snapshot metadata, and engine-neutral catalogs.
Open table format optimized for fast upserts and incremental pulls via merge-on-read or copy-on-write.
Row-oriented operational stores built for many short read/write transactions.
Lake storage plus ACID table formats and SQL engines — warehouse reliability at lake economics.
Extract-load-transform; raw data lands first and transforms run inside the target engine.
Extract-transform-load pipelines that shape data before it reaches the destination.
SQL functions computing aggregates over a row frame without collapsing rows (RANK, moving averages).
Directed acyclic graph — Spark stages and orchestrator workflows are both modeled as DAGs.
Spark's rule- and cost-based query optimizer producing the physical plan.
The Spark JVM that builds the DAG, schedules tasks, and collects results.
Worker JVM that runs Spark tasks on partitions and caches blocks.
Adding a random prefix to hot keys so a skewed partition splits into manageable pieces.
Querying a table as of an earlier snapshot using table-format versioning.
Under a network partition, a distributed store must sacrifice either consistency or availability.
Majority acknowledgment rule (R+W greater than N) keeping reads and writes consistent through failures.
Getting nodes to agree on one value or log despite crashes and partitions.
Leader-based consensus protocol replicating a log — the readable alternative to Paxos.
Keeping copies of data on multiple nodes for durability and read scale.
Splitting a dataset across nodes or partitions for parallel storage and processing.
The timestamp embedded in a record (when it happened) — the basis for correct windowing.
Records arriving after their window closed, handled via watermarks and allowed lateness.
Processing a stream as small bounded batches — Spark Structured Streaming's original model.
Spark's streaming API that treats a stream as an unbounded table queried incrementally.
Serving batch and realtime needs from one log-based stream pipeline.

Compressing vectors to fewer bits per dimension so indexes fit in memory.
Splitting documents into retrieval-sized passages for embedding and indexing.
Fluent model output unsupported by sources or training facts.
Policy layer filtering or constraining model inputs and outputs for safety and compliance.
First serving stage narrowing millions of items to hundreds for the ranker.
Recommending from interaction patterns alone; discovers well, suffers cold start.
No interaction history for new users or items; handled with content features and heuristics.
Weighted alternating least squares — matrix-factorization solver that weights unobserved pairs.
Friends-of-friends — social-graph candidate source for people recommendations.

Factorization machine plus shared-embedding DNN — the classic CTR model.
Gradient-boosted decision trees — strong tabular baseline but hard to fine-tune continually.
Click-through rate — probability a shown item is clicked; the core ads prediction.
Final serving stage applying business logic and filters the model should not own.
Continuous finetune-evaluate-deploy loop, shipped only on metric improvement.
Generative model that iteratively denoises random noise toward data, guided by conditioning.
Conv downsampling and upsampling denoiser backbone where cross-attention injects the prompt.
Attention where queries come from image features and keys and values from text embeddings.
Variational autoencoder — encoder-decoder latent generative model; fast and stable, lower fidelity.
Discrete tokenizer — CNN encoder, codebook quantization, decoder; turns images into tokens.
Latent diffusion model — diffusion run in a VAE-compressed latent space for tractability.

Deterministic sampler cutting diffusion inference from 1000 steps to about 20.
Sampling trick that strengthens prompt adherence without a separate classifier.
Generator versus discriminator adversarial training — fast one-pass generation, unstable training.
GAN with a layered latent space enabling fine-grained facial attribute editing.
GAN failure where the generator produces one plausible output regardless of input.

Contrastively trained image-text encoder pair enabling zero-shot scoring and multimodal conditioning.

Decoding that keeps the top partial sequences — deterministic, quality-leaning alternative to sampling.
Frechet inception distance — distributional image quality and diversity metric.
Frechet video distance over I3D features — captures temporal coherence per-frame metrics miss.
N-gram precision metric for translation and captioning.
N-gram recall metric for summarization.
Alignment-based translation metric adding recall and stemming to n-gram matching.
TF-IDF-weighted n-gram consensus metric for captioning against multiple references.
Mean average precision over classes or thresholds — standard detection and ranking metric.
Normalized discounted cumulative gain — ranking metric handling graded relevance.
Mean reciprocal rank — for retrieval with exactly one relevant item.
Fraction of relevant items present in the top k results.

1: Internal committee defense of YOUR project work — not external-style puzzles.
Bring: problem → constraints → 2–3 design options → tradeoff rationale → measured outcome.
Competency matrix is the rubric: map every claim to a matrix line.
Manager sponsorship + readiness review gate the attempt.
[WARN] Process details are reported, not officially documented.
2: Window functions compute per-row values over a frame without collapsing rows — the core difference from GROUP BY.
Canonical dedup: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY ts DESC, id DESC)`, keep rn=1 — one scan, deterministic ties.
Logical order: FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY/HAVING → windows → ORDER BY; WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups.
SARGable predicates only: `CAST(dt AS STRING)` full-scans; `dt = DATE '2024-01-01'` prunes partitions.
LEFT JOIN plus WHERE on the right table's column silently becomes an INNER JOIN — move it into ON.
Duplicate join keys fan out rows: a 1.1x key duplication silently doubles summed revenue.
CTEs get inlined and recomputed — Snowflake: `AS MATERIALIZED`; Spark: `CACHE TABLE`.
3: "File won't fit in memory" → generator: yield, don't return — dicts/sets are O(n) RAM, generators O(1).
Reach for Spark at >10 GB, multi-file/Parquet input, cross-dataset joins, or "distributed"; plain Python under ~1 GB.
Driver OOM: `collect()`/`toPandas()`. Executor OOM: skew, `repartition(1)` before a heavy stage, cache without MEMORY_AND_DISK.
UDF ladder: native 1× → pandas UDF ~2–5× (Arrow batches) → Python UDF ~10×+; use `F.when`, never a UDF, for conditionals.
Skew: diagnose via `groupBy(col).count().orderBy(desc("count"))` or a Spark UI straggler; fix by salting the hot key (16 buckets) + two-stage agg.
`repartition(n, col)` shuffles and balances; `coalesce(n)` skips the shuffle but can leave skew.
Cache only when reused ≥2× (`MEMORY_AND_DISK`, then `unpersist()`) — blind `.cache()` is a memory leak.
4: CAP forces the C-vs-A choice only under a network partition: CP refuses stale answers (ZooKeeper, etcd), AP serves possibly stale (Cassandra, DynamoDB).
Quorum rule: `R + W > N` forces read/write overlap; `W > N/2` prevents split-brain.
N=5 math: W=3/R=3 → 99.1% both paths; W=1/R=5 → ~99.999% writes but 59.0% reads.
Retries are mandatory → at-least-once delivery → duplicates guaranteed; idempotency keys, dedup tables, upserts make replays no-ops.
"Exactly-once" is effectively-once end-to-end: idempotent producer + transactional offsets + a sink that participates in commit.
Wall clocks lie across machines — order with event time + watermarks; LWW silently discards concurrent updates.
2PC is atomic but blocking (crashed coordinator holds locks); sagas chain local transactions with compensations.
5: Draw the spine: sources → ingestion → storage → transform → serve, plus cross-cutting orchestration, catalog, observability, security — mention unprompted.
Ingestion carries no business logic; log-based CDC (binlog/WAL → Debezium → Kafka) is the OLTP default — captures hard deletes; polling misses them, triggers slow every write.
Medallion invariants: bronze immutable raw (replay insurance), silver deduped/typed/validated with a quality gate → quarantine, gold curated for BI/ML; skip layers without trust boundaries.
Declare grain first — "one row per order line"; model the business process, not the source system.
Star schema for BI, Data Vault for auditable multi-source integration, OBT for zero-join ML/single-consumer scans.
SCD2: the fact's surrogate FK pins it to the dimension version true at event time; expire + insert in one transaction.
Data contracts: versioned, machine-enforced in producer CI — a renamed column is caught at build time, not as NULLs in gold.
6: Batch answers "what is true given all data up to now" (bounded); streaming "what is true right now" (unbounded) — the trade is latency vs reprocessing/state cost, not throughput.
Escalation path: batch → micro-batch (Spark SS ~500 ms floor) → true streaming (Flink/Kafka Streams 10–100 ms); each step up is a permanent tax: state ops, checkpoints, watermark tuning.
Only event time is reproducible; processing time is for lag monitoring.
Watermark `W = maxObservedEventTime − allowedLateness` (typ. 20 s–5 min); a window emits when W passes its end; W = min across partitions, so one idle source stalls everything.
Late events: within allowedLateness → re-accumulate and re-fire (retraction); beyond → side output or dead-letter queue.
State (windows, join buffers, dedup keys) needs a TTL or it grows forever.
Exactly-once exists only end-to-end: replayable source + exactly-once state + transactional/idempotent sink — else at-least-once plus dedupe.
7: Four generations, each failure mode the next's feature list: EDW → lake → cloud DW → lakehouse; answer "why the transition" with failure mechanisms, not product names.
Lakes failed structurally (60–85% of big-data projects abandoned): no atomic commits, no schema enforcement, no compaction, no governance.
Lakehouse = Parquet + transactional table format + object storage + catalog + any engine — the format + catalog is the platform.
Cloud DW disaggregation (micro-partitions ~16 MB with min/max pruning, isolated virtual warehouses, per-second auto-suspend) vs shared-nothing rebalancing cost.
Lakehouse contribution: schema-on-write with late binding — enforce at commit, evolve without rewriting files.
ELT displaced ETL where storage/compute decoupled; ETL survives at trust boundaries (PII masking before load, cross-region).
Cost rule: utilization <30% → per-second auto-suspend; >60% sustained → always-on/reserved; watch egress and per-TB-scanned ($6.25/TB BigQuery).
8: Converging from opposite origins; the deepest difference is storage ownership: Snowflake abstracts it (bundled bill), Databricks makes your lake the source of truth in your bucket.
Snowflake: warehouses XS→6XL auto-suspend to zero, ~16 MB micro-partitions with min/max pruning, Time Travel + zero-copy cloning.
Databricks: Spark + Photon (C++ vectorized) over your S3 with the Delta ACID log — Photon is why its SQL got competitive.
Billing: credits bundle IaaS (60 s minimum); DBUs stack on the VM bill — never compare list rates, model 3-year all-in TCO (worked example: ~15% DBX edge, entirely assumption-driven).
All-purpose ($0.55) vs jobs ($0.15) DBU misclassification is ~3×.
Fit: SQL/BI + turnkey ops → Snowflake; ML/GPU/code-first/continuous streaming → Databricks; governance parity, openness favors Unity Catalog.

Lock-in: Snowflake locks data gravity, Databricks locks workflows; Iceberg + one REST catalog (Open Catalog/Polaris/UC) is the neutral layer — vendor benchmarks contradict by workload shape, so run a 2-week PoC.
9: A table format adds what Parquet lacks: atomic commits, updates/deletes, schema/partition evolution, and pruning metadata over immutable files.
Delta is a log: `_delta_log` JSON commits + Parquet checkpoint every 10th commit, optimistic concurrency, Deletion Vectors since 2.x.
Iceberg is a tree: catalog CAS pointer → metadata.json → manifest list → manifests → data files, with pruning summaries at every level.
Hidden partitioning: transforms (`days(ts)`, `bucket(16, user_id)`) live in the spec — partition evolution is metadata-only, no rewrite.
Hudi is a timeline of instants (the WAL) over file groups; CoW rewrites bases, MoR appends logs until compaction folds them.
Delete cost ladder: CoW rewrite → position deletes → DV bitmaps → MoR log records — write cost falls, read cost rises. GDPR deletes: DVs make them KB-scale.
Time travel = replay; only VACUUM/expire_snapshots/clean truly deletes. Benchmarks are vendor-shaped — decide from estate: Iceberg multi-engine, Delta Databricks, Hudi keyed CDC.
10: Spark is a batch engine that grew micro-batch streaming; Flink is a streaming engine where batch is just a bounded stream — scheduling, state, failure handling follow from that.
Latency floors: Spark ~batch interval (0.5–10 s, p99 pinned by batch commit); Flink ~10 ms record-at-a-time.
Spark pipeline: lazy plans → Catalyst (pushdown, join choice, whole-stage codegen) → stages cut at shuffle boundaries; AQE coalesces and skew-splits at runtime; RocksDB state store default since 4.0.
Flink exactly-once = rewindable source + async barrier snapshot (Chandy–Lamport) + TwoPhaseCommittingSink (pre-commit at checkpoint, commit on notifyCheckpointComplete).
Unaligned checkpoints under backpressure: barriers overtake in-flight buffers — larger snapshots, steady duration.
AQE skew rule: partition > 256 MB and > 5× median → split into ~64 MB subtasks (512 GB straggler: 60 min → 8 min, −87%); salting is the fallback costing two shuffles.
Set TTL on every keyed Flink op — unbounded state is the #1 production killer; checkpoint interval bounds 2PC deliverable latency.
11: Catalyst: rule-based logical optimization (pushdown, pruning, folding) + cost-based physical planning; without `ANALYZE TABLE`, `sizeInBytes` defaults huge so auto-broadcast never fires at compile time.
AQE re-plans at each shuffle boundary from actual map-output stats — default since 3.2: coalesce toward ~64 MB, skew-join split, SMJ→BHJ/SHJ switch; useless without an Exchange.
AQE skew-join split fires only above BOTH thresholds: > 5× median partition AND > 256 MB — joins only; groupBy skew needs salting.
Join choice = one threshold + honest stats: broadcast ≤ 10 MB (misestimate → driver OOM), SHJ on hint, SMJ the robust default.
Size partitions ≈ shuffle bytes ÷ 128–256 MB — the 200 default is wrong in both directions; over-provision and let AQE coalesce (it cannot split ordinary oversized partitions).
Unified memory (fraction 0.6): storage evicts, execution spills; G1GC for ≥4–8 GB heaps; GC > 10–15% of task time = allocation churn.
Diagnose from the UI: max ≫ p50 → skew; spill counters → memory; fix data shape before knobs.
12: Three messaging models: queue (one consumer, ack-then-delete), pub/sub (fan-out, no replay), log (Kafka: partitioned, replayable, consumer-owned offsets — replay is an offset reset).
Ordering is per-partition only: `hash(key) % partitions` gives per-entity order; changing partition count silently breaks the key map.
ISR = replicas current within `replica.lag.time.max.ms` (30 s); high watermark = highest offset replicated to all ISR — consumers read only up to HW.
Durability recipe: `acks=all` + RF=3 + `min.insync.replicas=2` + `unclean.leader.election.enable=false`; ISR shrunk to 1 → explicit `NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS`, not silent loss.
Exactly-once stops at Kafka's edge: idempotent producer (PID + sequence, default since 3.0) + transactions + `read_committed`; across boundaries use the outbox — never dual-write.
Rebalance-proofing: cooperative-sticky assignor (KIP-429) + static membership + `max.poll.records` finishing inside `max.poll.interval.ms` (5 min default).
KRaft replaced ZooKeeper (removed in 4.0, 2025); schema evolution `FULL_TRANSITIVE` on shared topics; tiered storage decouples retention from broker disk.
13: Six quality dimensions are the shared vocabulary: accuracy, completeness, freshness, validity, uniqueness, consistency — every tool (GE, dbt, Soda) maps to them.
Test pyramid: unit tests every PR, data tests every pipeline run, expensive reconciliations daily/before publish, production monitoring continuous.
Observability = metrics (what broke) + logs (where) + lineage (what else); OpenLineage/Marquez bounds the blast radius.
Gate failure → circuit breaker: publish to staging, promote atomically — consumers keep last-known-good; alert when quarantine rate exceeds ~1%.
SLO math: 99% on-time over 30 daily runs → error budget 0.3 runs → page on the first miss; thresholds come from budget math, not complaints.
Idempotent backfill: DELETE + INSERT per partition or MERGE — never blind append; same input must give same output.
Incident loop: alert → classify → contain → fix → backfill → verify → blameless postmortem; every incident ends as a new automated check.
14: Five sources, five jobs: the wiki explains concepts, the handbook curates, Start Data Engineering builds (100+ posts), DET gives community signal, DEC practitioner benchmarks.
Canonical reading list = 4 books + 2 papers — Fundamentals of DE, DDIA 2e, Kimball, Learning Spark 2e; GFS, Lakehouse CIDR — not the handbook's 25-book firehose.
Hold a 1:2 read-to-build ratio: tutorial hell (the 40th Spark video) compounds to zero; if you can't whiteboard your build's failure modes, you watched, not learned.
Attach every drill to one build spine — API → ingest → lake → transform+DQ → serve → ops — one repo, layers added weekly, reps compound.
Pick ONE portfolio archetype (batch lakehouse, streaming, CDC, DQ-gated, LLM) and finish it; a small finished repo with a tradeoffs README beats three half-cloned tutorials.
Drill 15 — a 5-minute walkthrough of your own design doc — IS the A3 architecture screen; rehearse until 5 minutes feels short.
15: The internal design round probes YOUR project plus hypothetical extensions; the committee scores narrative + evidence against the competency matrix.

Six steps: Clarify (SLA first, 3–5 min) → Estimate → High-level design (SLA on every hop) → Tradeoffs (per arrow: alternative, why rejected, one number) → Ops & failure (unprompted) → Evolution (precomputed 10x).
Evidence ledger replaces STAR: claim → story → artifact → metric → matrix line; 4–5 proof stories, 90 s each, "I" never "we".
Capacity math before architecture; your pipeline's real numbers beat textbook figures — 100k ev/s × 500 B = 4.32 TB/day, RF=3 ≈ 13 TB → 6 brokers × 4 TB, 48 partitions ≈ 1.04 MB/s each.
Exactly-once is not correctness: checkpoints/2PC are processing semantics — late joins, timezones, fraud need dedup windows and reconciliation.
Migration invariant: no consumer ever sees wrong data — waves ordered by consumer, parity gate 7 consecutive days < 0.01% delta.
English delivery is scored (B2 gates staffing); honest "I don't know — here's how I'd reason" reads senior.
16: The skeleton is the transferable asset: clarify requirements → frame as ML task → data → model → eval → system design + deployment/monitoring — one rehearsal covers any prompt.
Model choice is requirements arithmetic, not fashion: one-pass latency → GAN/VAE, ceiling quality → diffusion, resolution at scale → AR, video economics → latent diffusion.
Exhaust retrieval + prompts before finetuning: finetuning can't cite sources and needs constant retraining; RAFT only when retrieval is fixed and answers are still bad.
RAG pipeline: parse → chunk (500 chars, 200 overlap) → embed → ANN-index; size it explicitly — 5M pages → 40M chunks, +20%/yr.
Retrieval quality is the ceiling: a better LLM cannot fix bad chunks.
Pair offline metrics (BLEU, CIDEr, CLIPScore, FID/FVD, DINO) with online business metrics (CTR, adoption, cost per user) — naming both unprompted is the scoring behavior.
Deployment is a named stage: safety chain, serving, monitoring, retraining loops — users re-rolling seeds quietly multiplies GPU spend.
17: All 11 chapters share one 7-step skeleton: clarify → frame as ML task → data prep → model development → evaluate → deploy/serve → monitor.
The load-bearing move is business goal → ML objective with failure modes named: clicks reward clickbait, completions bias short videos → maximize relevant watch time.
Model ladder: popularity baseline → LR → DNN → ensemble only if needed; GBDT is rejected in continual-learning systems — no fine-tuning, retrain from scratch.
Metric elimination chain: MRR ignores post-first hits, recall@k drowns under millions of relevant items, precision@k is rank-blind → nDCG or mAP.
Serving skeleton: candidate generation (ANN above ~millions, inverted index, FoF) → ranking (feature store: static batch + dynamic) → re-ranking — business rules live in re-rank, never the model.
Observed-pairs-only MF loss hits zero with all-ones embeddings — weight unobserved pairs (WALS); calibrate ad pCTRs (NCE < 1 vs background CTR) or the auction breaks.
Freshness is a design constraint: ad click models need ~5-minute updates; Gmail Smart Compose: decoder-only, pretrain + finetune on 1B emails, deterministic beam search under ~100 ms.
18: Translation = seq2seq → encoder-decoder Transformer: bidirectional encoder, causally-masked decoder with cross-attention; chosen for variable-length I/O and source understanding.
Scope first: 4 languages (EN/ES/KO/FR), auto language detection (encoder-only classifier routes the fleet), inputs ≤ 1,000 words, 300M sentence pairs.
Two-stage training: masked-LM pretraining (next-token would let the encoder leak the answer) then supervised next-token finetuning; start from T5/BART checkpoints to skip stage 1.
Keep preprocessing that preserves grammar; drop legacy lowercasing/stemming/stop-words; subword BPE with `</w>` boundary tokens solves vocabulary size and OOV.
Placeholder named entities (ENTITY_1) in, restored after decoding — models choke on uncommon proper nouns.
Beam search, not stochastic sampling — determinism is a feature in translation.
Evaluate three ways: BLEU (precision, punishes rewording), ROUGE (recall), METEOR (synonyms, best human correlation) + online feedback; never trust BLEU alone.
19: Requirements before architecture: text-in/text-out, English-only, strict safety, ≥ 4096-token context, follow-ups in session, 80K (instruction, answer) pairs → decoder-only LLM.

Three stages, three jobs: pretraining (trillions of tokens, 1000s GPUs, months) buys knowledge; SFT (10K–100K demos) turns continuer into responder; RLHF (100K–1M comparisons → reward model → PPO/DPO) aligns.
Data quality inverts across stages: trillions of low-quality web tokens → small expert demonstrations → ranked comparisons; rank, never score — annotator numbers drift.
The 4096-token requirement forces RoPE-style positional encoding — absolute encodings trained at 512 break at long context.
Decoding default for open-ended chat: top-p/nucleus + tuned temperature (modern practice 0.1–1.5); greedy/beam loop in dialogue.
Evaluation is four layers: perplexity baseline, task benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval), safety benchmarks (RealToxicityPrompts, CrowS-Pairs, TruthfulQA), human + Arena-style online.
Safety enforced at inference on both directions: input safety filter, prompt enhancer, output evaluator routing failures to the rejection generator; session management supplies follow-up context.
20: Captioning = translation where the image is the source language: image encoder → embedding sequence → decoder-only Transformer → caption token by token.
ViT-style encoder emitting per-patch tokens beats a single global vector — attention wants sequences, and a global summary loses local detail.

Data quality dominates at 400M noisy pairs: dedup via perceptual hash/CLIP, CLIP relevance filter (~0.25 threshold), LLM-summarize long captions, drop <256×256, resize+center-crop preserving aspect ratio.
Reuse pretrained weights both sides: GPT-2/Llama decoder, CLIP/ViT encoder; joint finetuning with next-token cross-entropy.
Beam search at serving — quality, determinism ("same image, same caption"), coherence; 1–2 s latency makes it affordable.
Ambiguous images are a designed skip path: cumulative probability below the confidence threshold disables the suggestion; post-processing neutralizes biased terms.
Evaluate with CIDEr over multiple reference captions — TF-IDF vectorize, cosine-similarity, average; blind spots: novel-but-correct phrasing, word-order semantics.
21: RAG = offline pipeline (parse → chunk → embed → index) + online loop (query → embed → ANN → prompt → LLM); tune retrieval before blaming the model.
Pick RAG over finetuning when knowledge changes (~20%/yr) and answers must cite sources; finetuning can't stay current and produces no references.
Varied layouts need AI-based parsing — layout detection + OCR per box in reading order; fixed-template rule-based parsers break.
Chunk math drives capacity: 5M pages × 1,500 chars, chunk 500 with 200 overlap → 5 text + 3 image chunks/page ≈ 40M chunks.
Shared embedding space is the invariant: same encoder for chunks and queries; CLIP or caption-then-embed aligns images.
Exact search is O(N×D) — 40M comparisons per query; ANN (clustering, LSH, HNSW) is mandatory at this scale.
Evaluate the RAG triad — context relevance, faithfulness, answer relevance; one aggregate score hides which half broke. RAFT-finetune (golden + distractor docs) only after retrieval is fixed.
22: Requirements select the model: faces only, 1024×1024, <1s latency, 70k licensed images, balanced demographics, attribute control as stretch goal.
GAN over diffusion/autoregressive: single forward pass meets <1s; the structured latent space enables later StyleGAN attribute control — quality traded for speed, instability accepted.
Data prep: quality filter, flip/rotate/color augmentation, resize to 1024 with pixels normalized −1..1 (drives the Tanh output), classifier-tagged demographic rebalancing.
Alternating freeze-train is the core discipline: train D a few iters, freeze, train G — imbalance is the root of all three classic failures.
Three failures, named fixes: vanishing gradients → WGAN critic; mode collapse → unrolled GAN; non-convergence (D accuracy → 50%) → different learning rates + noise into D.
Sampling: random over the full latent Gaussian — diversity matters for faces; truncation trades diversity for realism.
Evaluate IS (higher-better), FID (lower-better), and pairwise human votes — automated metrics misalign with judgment.
23: Requirements: 5M natural-scene images, unconditional generation, 1024²–2048² output, ~5 s per image — not real-time.
Latency math picks the model: pixel-level autoregression is O(N²) (~1M steps at 1024²) and diffusion is O(T·N²) (minutes); chunk tokens at 64×64 px/token cut it to 256 steps — seconds.
VQ-VAE tokenizer: CNN encoder → nearest-neighbor codebook quantizer → transposed-conv decoder; discrete latents kill posterior collapse and shrink the prediction space to k tokens.
Stage I losses weighted: reconstruction (MSE) + quantization (stop-gradient) + perceptual (VGG features) + adversarial (patch-based); MSE-only shows artifacts at high res.
Nearest-neighbor lookup has no gradient — straight-through gradient copies decoder gradients to the encoder.
Two independently trained models composed at inference: tokenizer (reconstruction) + generator (decoder-only Transformer, next-token cross-entropy over cached sequences).

24: Requirements drive decisions: 1024×1024, ~500M pairs, ≤128-word prompts, ~10 s SLA, broad scope, fairness and safety.
Diffusion over autoregressive: AR simpler to train, diffusion wins fine detail plus a sampling-steps dial — pay implementation complexity for quality.
Training is four steps: sample t from 1..1000, closed-form noise to x_t, condition on text + timestep, predict the noise ε (not x₀) with MSE loss.
U-Net vs DiT: cross-attention is the steering layer — queries from image features, keys/values from text-encoder (CLIP/T5) embeddings.
Sampling's two fixes: classifier-free guidance buys prompt adherence; DDIM cuts 1,000 steps to ~20 for the latency budget.

Method scorecard: textual inversion low effectiveness (one token embedding), LoRA low-rank delta at MB storage, DreamBooth full-parameter finetune — highest identity, GB storage, ~15 min.

Rare-token identifier `[V]`: common words carry meanings to overwrite, random strings fragment — rare tokens are distinct yet cohesive.

26: Requirements: 5-second 720p (1280×720) at 24 FPS silent videos, minutes of latency acceptable, ~100M video–caption pairs, >6000 H100s.

LDM is the enabling trick: VAE compresses 8× spatial and 8× temporal — 512× fewer values to denoise.
Precompute and cache latents (~200 TB for 100M videos): per-step VAE encoding would stall every training iteration; re-caption with LLaMa3-Video/LLaVA for alignment.
DiT over U-Net for new builds: 3D patchify, Transformer scaling with data + compute — Sora and Movie Gen both chose it.
Evaluate three axes: frame quality (FID/IS — blind to motion), temporal consistency (FVD, lower-better, over I3D features), alignment (CLIP similarity) + pairwise human votes.
